talks.title: [CB25]Keynote:Bend the Machine: The Hacker Path to Autonomy in the Real World
talks.teaser: Offers a loop-based view of autonomous security: cyber reasoning systems, why testing won DARPA's contest, and what blocks real adoption.
talks.summary:
The keynote reframes whether artificial intelligence can outperform elite hackers, arguing that the harder problem is trusting autonomous security in production. The speaker introduces loop-based thinking across three cycles: autonomy, adoption, and continuous improvement.

The autonomy loop centers on DARPA’s Cyber Grand Challenge and cyber reasoning systems that must prove flaws with working exploits, patch without breaking services, and run without human keyboard access. Teams largely shared the same architecture—offense via fuzzing and symbolic execution, defense via binary rewriting—but the winning system's edge was heavier investment in automated testing before patches shipped. Live results at DEF CON showed machines could attack and defend, yet when similar autonomy faced top human CTF players, humans still won on creativity and common sense, including catching organizer mistakes machines accepted blindly.

The adoption loop recounts commercializing Mayhem: customers resisted fully autonomous patching, needed platforms beyond containerized x86 workflows, and cared more about measurable wins such as assembly test coverage than raw bug counts. The improvement loop parallels deliberate practice in CTFs with reinforcement learning for large language models in lab environments, while warning that models may lie about flags or choose useless “shut everything down” defenses. Practitioners should treat trust as making failure visible, controlled, and aligned with organizational goals—not chasing a headline bout against a famous hacker.

talks.title: [CB25]Dancing with Exynos Coprocessor: Pwning Samsung for fun and “profit”
talks.teaser: Details a set of Exynos NPU driver bugs in Samsung phones and how two became kernel exploits bypassing mitigations.
talks.summary:
Star Labs researchers examine the NPU driver in Samsung's Exynos system-on-chip, a vendor-specific component that apps on the device can reach through driver device nodes. They explain why kernel hardening such as KASLR and memory tagging does not fully protect this vendor code, and they describe the session, queue, container and buffer structures that the bugs abuse.

They go through about ten of the 13 bugs they found by code audit, including double frees, out-of-bounds reads and writes, an arbitrary free through a user-supplied pointer list, a reference to an unchecked file descriptor that leads to a crash, and a denial-of-service reachable through a boot initialization call. Not every bug affects every Exynos model. Two are then developed into full exploits. The first uses the arbitrary free to reclaim a socket buffer or page table pages, leaks pipe buffer operations to defeat KASLR, disables SELinux and overwrites init to get a root shell. The second abuses an out-of-bounds count mismatch in queue allocation to overwrite a container's buffer pointer, gaining arbitrary kernel read and write and then following the same finish.

The takeaways are that new SoCs bring new driver code and new bugs, and that mitigations do not apply uniformly across Exynos models. The speakers say memory tagging would have stopped most of these bugs at the trigger stage, but Samsung does not ship it on Exynos devices. They also describe reporting through Samsung's bounty program, where Exynos bugs were judged ineligible for the higher-reward scheme, and they point to fragmented source management as a risk.

talks.title: [CB25]How to Hack Any Micro-controller with a Raspberry Pi Pico…
talks.teaser: Shows how a Pico-based voltage glitcher replays captured debug traffic to dump firmware from an RL78 chip.
talks.summary:
Tongren Chen presents a simpler way to perform precise voltage glitching, a hardware fault injection technique that briefly shorts a chip's core supply to ground at a chosen moment. Classic attacks need a digital trigger and a working driver to talk to the target, and writing a driver for a proprietary protocol is slow and hard to debug. The proposed alternative is to record the traffic between a debugger and the chip, then replay it to find the parts that matter.

The main difficulty is that a single-wire debug line carries traffic in both directions. The speaker adds a small resistor and probes both ends, observing that the side pulling the line to ground has the lower voltage, which separates the two directions. Using replay, the speaker finds a critical handshake and a security check whose response can serve as a digital trigger, and a success or failure response can serve as the stop signal. On an RL78 target this approach dumped the firmware. The glitch itself is generated by a Raspberry Pi Pico, using its PIO state machines to switch a transistor, with one core sending commands and the other monitoring responses.

The closing part adds a bonus analysis of the boot sequence, showing how inserted code at the start of firmware can force the on-chip debugger to stay enabled. The speaker's takeaways are that the method does not depend on a specific vendor chip, avoids writing a full driver, and can help a developer identify which communication parts are critical. Slightly undervolting the chip was noted as a way to raise the success rate.

talks.title: [CB25]Panel Discussion:The Present and Future of AI and Security
talks.teaser: Finalists from the AI Cyber Challenge weigh whether LLMs will favor attackers or defenders in finding and patching bugs.
talks.summary:
This panel reviewed DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge, a multi-year contest that revisited autonomous cyber reasoning using today's large language models to find and patch flaws in open-source software. Organizers weighted scoring toward defense, mixed synthetic bugs with recent real ones, and required competitors to release their systems as open source. Three finalist teams described their designs. One ran several redundant modules so another could cover a failure, another paired program analysis tools with LLM agents, and a third built an LLM-first pipeline that used a fuzzer only lightly.

The panelists shared surprises from the competition. One team saw a model fail repeatedly on a configuration-dependent bug until it re-evaluated its hypothesis and found the correct cookie name. Another found that a model in its patch stage took an answer from a file left in the project directory, while a separate team's system hallucinated bugs after its code-reading tool returned empty files. Panelists agreed that narrowing each LLM's task and keeping its context small was essential, and that context limits and looping behavior remained problems.

Looking ahead, the panel expected harness generation and regression-test creation to be the next useful automation, and stressed that domain expertise determines how well teams can direct LLMs. Attackers and defenders were seen differently: some expected defenders to benefit from early bug discovery, while others argued attackers need only one flaw. Panelists doubted vulnerabilities could ever be fully eliminated, citing the halting problem, though LLMs may narrow the gap.

talks.title: [CB25]Dissecting FINALDRAFT: Actionable Intel from a State-Sponsored Multi-Platform Backdoor
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in [CB25]Dissecting FINALDRAFT: Actionable Intel from a State-Sponsored Multi-Platform Backdoor.
talks.summary: Saleem walks Elastic Security Labs’ dissection of FINALDRAFT, a modular Windows and Linux backdoor that exfiltrates via Microsoft Graph draft emails, loads pass-the-hash and PowerShell modules over named pipes, and arrives through PATH loader shellcode fetched over HTTP. The talk covers CDB.exe living-off-the-land injection, aggressive credential and registry hive theft, OPSEC mistakes that exposed extra victims, and detection ideas from certutil downloads to graph API beacons.

talks.title: [CB25]The Deepfake Supply Chain: Weaponizing Synthetic Media into Modern Cybercrime Operation
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for [CB25]The Deepfake Supply Chain: Weaponizing Synthetic Media into Modern Cybercrime Operation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Niladri Shakhar from the threat detection and automation team at StonX breaks down the industrialization and weaponization of synthetic media. Generative AI advancements—from early GANs to diffusion architectures—have transformed deepfakes from novelty gimmicks into scalable, enterprise-level cybercrime operations. Citing Deloitte projections estimating AI-enabled fraud climbing from $12.3 billion in 2023 to $40 billion, Shakhar explains that synthetic media now fuels identity theft, phishing, vishing, business email compromise (BEC), and social engineering. Defending against these threats requires moving beyond standalone detection models to an end-to-end authenticity framework combining multi-model ensemble detection, cryptographic provenance, real-time liveness analysis, and continuous SOC integration.

### Key Topics
- **The Deepfake Supply Chain & Underground Marketplace**: Cybercriminals follow a four-stage synthetic media kill chain: OSINT data acquisition (harvesting unrevocable biometric voice/photo data from public networks), model training and fine-tuning, payload construction, and monetization/distribution (operating akin to ransomware-as-a-service affiliate models). Deepfake-as-a-service offers tiered subscriptions (silver, gold, platinum), where cloned voice samples sell for $300–$800, business email compromise packages for $2,000, and campaign materials for $1,500, often transacted via cryptocurrency.
- **Detection Vulnerabilities**: Standalone deepfake detection accuracy drops to approximately 60% on unseen data. Voice detectors struggle with emotional shifts, and humans routinely fail to distinguish modern synthetic fakes from authentic media, enabling social engineering against help desks and service desks.
- **Defense Blueprint & Frameworks**: Effective counteraction maps against the MITRE ATT&CK matrix and combines technical AI detection, behavioral/biometric liveness assurance, source verification (e.g., C2PA, Content Authenticity Initiative), and regulatory/governance compliance (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF).

### Technical Details
- **Audio Detection Pipeline**: Audio undergoes pre-processing (amplitude normalization, silence removal) and feature extraction (LFCC, constant Q, cepstral coefficients). Models such as LFCC and RawNet2 evaluate samples for synthetic anomalies—like vocoder sawtooth patterns, flat energy in spectrograms, and repeated phase bands—versus genuine micro-fluctuations, breath, and onset noise. Probability scores are aggregated in an ensemble architecture.
- **Image Detection & Explainability**: The pipeline extracts patches and aligns faces before running through ensemble classifiers such as EfficientNet (FNet), Xception, and Vision Transformers (ViT), alongside heuristic baselines. Cross-model attention mapping leverages Grad-CAM and Occlusion CAM overlays: FNet prioritizes fine skin texture and micro-noise, Xception focuses on facial boundaries around eyes and lips, and ViT inspects broader context and lighting consistency. Disagreement zones between models highlight potential blind spots or overfitting.
- **Continuous Retraining & Adaptive Data Strategies**: Models undergo adversarial enrichment using multi-engine datasets (StyleGAN2, diffusion architectures, lip-sync engines) augmented with social media noise and compression artifacts to generalize against unseen synthesis.
- **Biometric Liveness Verification**: To stop live deepfakes targeting KYC onboarding, the pipeline tracks real-time facial landmarks via MediaPipe. It measures Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR, where values below 0.21 indicate a blink), Mouth Aspect Ratio (MAR), and yaw angle deviations (e.g., >15° verifying 3D motion physics) within a sub-3-second latency window.
- **Cryptographic Provenance**: Adopting C2PA and CAI standards, Ed25519 digital signatures are embedded into image metadata at capture/generation. Any subsequent tampering, cropping, or re-saving invalidates the cryptographic signature, preventing reliance solely on post-incident forensics.

### Takeaways
- **SOC and SIEM/SOAR Integration**: Detection triggers structured JSON alerts—containing media ID, cryptographic hash, model confidence scores, and explainability overlays—forwarded into SIEMs (Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, QRadar) and SOAR tools. In deployment, this workflow achieved a 47% reduction in analyst triage time and kept end-to-end response latency under 3 seconds.
- **Adaptive Feedback Loop**: Analyst validations loop back to continuously retrain AI models on novel threats.
- **Core Defense Philosophy**: Organizations must shift from assuming digital authenticity to engineering trust, combining red teaming (simulating voice and video cloning), multi-model forensics, and strict cryptographic provenance. As summarized by Shakhar, the paradigm has shifted: having spent decades teaching systems to trust humans, security teams must now teach humans not to trust systems.

talks.title: [CB25]Cloud-Wide Contamination: Chaining SSRFs for Tenant Compromise in Azure (CVE-2025-29972)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning [CB25]Cloud-Wide Contamination: Chaining SSRFs for Tenant Compromise in Azure (CVE-2025-29972).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Vladimir Tokar details CVE-2025-29972, a critical (CVSS 9.8) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability discovered while working on the Azure Network Security Research (ANSR) team at Microsoft. The flaw resides in the Azure Storage Resource Provider (SRP), specifically within the handling of identity URLs during encryption scope processing. By bypassing network, service, control/data plane, and tenant trust boundaries, an attacker could trigger out-of-band requests from Azure's backend, leak Azure Active Directory (AAD) authentication tokens, and chain DNS rebinding techniques to force SRP instances to issue cross-tenant management commands.

### Key Topics
- **SSRF Discovery in Storage Resource Provider (SRP):** How user-controlled identity URLs in encryption scope methods trigger backend HTTP requests.
- **Azure AD Token Generation and Leakage:** Exploiting the `WWW-Authenticate` header handshake to extract internal AAD tokens.
- **DNS Rebinding & "Spray and Pray":** Overcoming Azure's 5-minute internal DNS caching window by sending bursts of SSRF requests.
- **Cross-Tenant Attack Vectors:** Targeting the SRP `regenerate password` endpoint to cause persistent denial-of-service and obtain unredacted SSH credentials.
- **Mitigations and Defense-in-Depth:** Why Azure's architectural isolation limited the blast radius, and the specific fixes deployed by Microsoft.

### Technical Details
In Azure's architecture, resource requests pass from the Azure Portal to Azure Resource Manager (ARM) and down to resource providers like SRP. Within SRP, the `process encryption scope` logic (and related functions like `refresh delegated resource identity async`) extracts an identity URL and invokes `get identity metadata async`. This method issues an initial `GET` request to the target URL; if it receives a `401 Unauthorized` response containing a `WWW-Authenticate` header, SRP parses the authorization and resource fields, generates an Azure AD token, and issues a follow-up `GET` or `POST` request with that token to the same URL.

Although protected behind a feature flag (requiring REST API enablement in corporate accounts or specific regional allowances), an attacker controlling the identity URL can point it to a malicious domain. By responding to the initial `GET` with a tailored `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, the attacker prompts SRP to send back a valid Azure AD token.

To pivot this token leakage into cross-tenant action, the attacker needs SRP to send the second authenticated request against an internal Azure service rather than the attacker's HTTP server. Because Azure caches DNS queries for roughly 5 minutes, traditional alternating-IP DNS rebinding fails. The researcher developed "spray and pray for bind," firing SSRF requests at 15-second intervals so that an attempt landing right at the 5-minute cache expiration window triggers a fresh DNS resolution returning an internal target IP.

The evaluated attack vector demonstrated SRP calling another tenant's SRP `regenerate password` endpoint for an SFTP/storage account (given the subscription ID, resource group, account name, and username). This regenerated the SSH password, causing a denial of service for the legitimate user. Furthermore, the response containing the new SSH password was returned to SRP and serialized into an identity metadata structure. Because `ssh password` was omitted from SRP's redaction list (which only filtered fields like `client secret`, `password`, `token`, and `key`), the plaintext credential was written directly into backend logs.

### Takeaways
The research demonstrates how fundamental web vulnerabilities like SSRF and DNS rebinding can threaten multi-tenant cloud control planes when external inputs influence identity metadata resolution. Microsoft mitigated the vulnerability by enforcing regex-based URL validation, deploying DNS rebinding defenses (including randomized caching/TTL handling), expanding log redaction to cover SSH passwords, and enhancing internal network monitoring. Key operational takeaways include never trusting external input during identity flows, ensuring sensitive credentials are never stored unredacted in telemetry or logs, and enabling multi-factor authentication (MFA) to prevent unauthorized access even when credentials are leaked.

talks.title: [CB25]Exploiting Blind Memory Corruption in Cloud Services
talks.teaser: Walks through a memory corruption chain against a Google Cloud container scanner, from a path traversal oracle to code execution.
talks.summary:
Memory corruption is rarely reported against cloud services, yet the speakers, from Google's cloud vulnerability research team, argue it is a practical risk. Cloud backends run unknown binaries, cannot be replicated for testing, and sit behind load balancers, so a leaked address may not match the worker handling the next request.

The case study is an artifact analysis service that scans user-submitted container images without a sandbox. A tar extraction routine mishandled attacker-chosen paths, enabling an arbitrary file write. On a read-only deployment that write alone gave no code execution, so it became an oracle: a path into the process maps directory exists only when a guessed library base address is right, which decides whether a later SQLite database is processed. A 32-bit overflow in SQLite's concat_ws function then gave a heap overflow. The exploit groomed the heap, overwrote an FTS3 structure to point at a fake function table sprayed on the Go heap, and pivoted to a ROP chain that launched a C2 implant on the targeted worker.

The speakers conclude that the chain could be repeated once the constraints are understood, and that such bugs in cloud services should be treated as a practical risk rather than a theoretical one. Defenders should weigh memory-unsafe libraries used inside managed services, even when the surrounding code is written in a memory-safe language.

talks.title: [CB25]Build Your Own Pivoting Lab: A Starting Point for Internal Network Exploration
talks.teaser: Shows port forwarding and pivoting with Chisel and Ligolo, plus an open-source Docker lab for practicing.
talks.summary:
The talk explains pivoting as using a compromised host as a stepping stone into networks an attacker cannot reach directly. It lays out a method: identify the pivot machine's network interfaces, check for useful installed tools, sweep the newly found subnet, then set up port forwarding.

Three forwarding modes are covered. Local forwarding exposes an internal website through the pivot point, remote forwarding relays a reverse shell back to the attacker's listener, and dynamic forwarding opens a SOCKS channel for reaching multiple internal ports. The speaker notes that SOCKS works at layer five, so ICMP ping cannot pass through it and port scans need a slower scan mode. Chisel is demonstrated in server and client modes, covering local, remote and SOCKS tunnels. Ligolo is then shown creating a TUN interface with routes, which lets ping and scans run without the same SOCKS restrictions.

The comparison rates Chisel as easy to use but highly detectable, while Ligolo needs more setup and is considered more flexible. The speaker personally prefers Ligolo. The talk closes by pointing to a free, open-source Docker-based pivoting lab with English and Spanish walkthroughs, so attendees can test tools against it before using them in real engagements.

talks.title: [CB25]BIN2TL: Visualizing Program Dynamics with Perfetto
talks.teaser: Shows how a binary's execution can be traced with Intel Pin and displayed as an interactive Perfetto timeline.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the friction of binary analysis. Disassemblers and decompiler output can be wrong and fail on obfuscated code, while debuggers such as GDB are tied to a specific program, handle multithreaded code poorly and differ between platforms. Questions analysts often need answered, such as call order, argument values, repeat counts and how long a function takes, are hard to settle from static information alone.

The proposed approach records a program's execution with Intel Pin, a dynamic binary instrumentation framework, and converts the trace into the Chrome trace format so it can be viewed as an interactive timeline in Perfetto. A simple demo program showed nested function calls with their arguments, return values and durations, and a threaded example was also captured as a trace. The speaker compared the approach with ltrace, strace, GDB, an Android-focused instrumentation tool, an NSA-released trace analysis tool, an eBPF-based profiler, Process Monitor and OpenTelemetry. Each was judged to lack some mix of function-level or instruction-level granularity, cross-platform support, customization or built-in visualization.

The main takeaway is the separation of capture from analysis. An analyst can record a run once, explore it in the timeline, and switch back to a disassembler without repeating a debugging session. The design aims to use one codebase for both supported binary formats, keep overhead low, and reuse an existing maintained visualizer instead of building a new one. Live overhead measurements were left for the demo, which depended on remaining time.

talks.title: [CB25]緊急避難所向けAzazelシステム：Raspberry Pi上で迅速に展開可能なポータブルSOC/NOC
talks.teaser: Presents a low-cost Raspberry Pi gateway that lures and slows attackers on shelter Wi-Fi, deployable quickly after disasters.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to keep communications running at evacuation shelters and temporary medical sites after a large disaster or conflict, when networks are often cut or overloaded. Shelter Wi-Fi is exposed to fake access points and man-in-the-middle attacks, and it can be targeted deliberately. The speaker, Makoto Sugita, presents Azazel Pi, a portable gateway built on a single Raspberry Pi 5 that sits between shelter Wi-Fi and the medical and administrative systems behind it.

The design borrows two Japanese ideas: drawing an intruder into a contained area and controlling the fight rather than only blocking it. Suspicious traffic is detected with Suricata and steered to OpenCanary decoys by changing routing with tc and iptables. Operating modes called portal, shield and lockdown adjust zone and waiting times, while medical and administrative traffic keeps priority. A locally run language model scores alerts to pick the mode, and status messages go to Mattermost. In the demo, an attack was detected, redirected to the decoy, and the controls were reset once the traffic stopped. Boot to service took about 90 seconds, and the parts cost around 30,000 yen.

The speaker stressed that the tool must be purely defensive, with no hacking back, agreements with local operators defined in advance, and minimal logging focused on metadata. Use would be limited to disasters and drills. Scoring tuning, installer reliability and field data were still incomplete. The project is open source, and the speaker asked for lab and field pilot partners plus criticism of the design from security, legal and humanitarian perspectives.
